I do not find the instructor’s overall teaching and communication style professional. The scope and length of feedback appear to vary significantly by student; in some cases, feedback feels disproportionately brief, while in others it becomes unnecessarily long, which raises concerns about consistency. I also find the instructor’s communication skills limited, and student comments/feedback can be taken personally at times. Project-related guidance seems to depend heavily on the instructor’s momentary attitude, sometimes supportive, sometimes not supportive at all, making the process difficult to navigate and less predictable. Especially during juries/critiques, comments can shift from constructive feedback toward a belittling or humiliating tone; critiques can be excessively long, harsh, and occasionally include language that feels inappropriate for an academic setting (overly informal/abusive, even slang-like). This approach undermines respectful student–instructor communication, reduces motivation, and negatively affects the learning environment. Considering this is one of the most important courses in the curriculum, it is discouraging to work under such communication difficulties and demotivating conduct; I have not encountered a similarly unprofessional tone in my previous courses.

He is very patient and genuinely attentive to each student’s project. This year, he had to give feedback on a wide range of topics, yet he approached every project with the same level of care and interest. He is an excellent art director who is always focused on how a project can be improved and pushed further. While this constant drive to improve projects can sometimes feel tiring, it comes from a genuine desire for students to produce meaningful work. Overall, we are very lucky to have an instructor with such extensive experience and knowledge.

Oğuz Hoca is extremely knowledgeable and one of the most helpful instructors I have worked with. He always listens carefully to your ideas and supports you in developing them further. Rather than making you feel like an individual student, he makes you feel as if you are working as a team with him. I truly appreciate his insights, as he consistently comes up with the most creative and effective solutions.
course: artık projeler mezun olunca portfolyomuza koyabileceğimiz işler olmalı, işverenlere portfolyo gösterirken hiçbiri okul projelerine ilgi göstermiyor çünkü işlerine yaramıyor. şu an hem okul projelerini hem de portfolyoma koyabileceğim işverenin ilgisini çeken projeler yapmakla aynı anda uğraşıyorum.

I believe this course should be structured around projects that directly support building a strong graduation portfolio and should operate within a clearer professional framework; however, in my view, the current content and implementation fall far from that goal. Throughout the process, expectations, evaluation criteria, and the standards by which critiques are delivered have not been defined in a sufficiently clear and consistent manner. Since projects are evaluated by multiple instructors, inconsistencies in evaluation approaches can be visible even during juries. The process does not feel professionally managed in line with a studio discipline; instead, the ambiguity and resulting issues are at times communicated in a blaming tone and placed on students. Another challenge is that students are expected to produce high-level outcomes on topics that were not adequately taught or covered during the academic process. As a result, the studio environment, which should be constructive, often becomes toxic and demotivating, and critique tends to be destructive rather than supportive. In terms of grading, I do not perceive an equitable approach; it can create an impression of favoritism and student-dependent treatment. Under these conditions, my confidence in maintaining a professional academic environment, producing strong design outcomes, and protecting the university’s academic image is significantly weakened.

I expected much more from this course. Having a project that required working with the video medium during the middle of the semester significantly lowered my motivation, especially in my final year. Until the project proposal assignment, I did not feel that the coursework sufficiently supported or prepared us for the final project. Otherwise, it is very possible for this course to turn an already stressful final year into one of the most demotivating periods of the entire undergraduate experience.

In terms of the course structure, the timeline was poorly balanced. Some projects were given unnecessarily long periods, while others were rushed, which made the overall structure feel disorganized. The first project, in particular, felt unnecessary and overly personal to be graded. Additionally, the presentations were excessively long and not presented in a clear or instructional manner, which reduced their effectiveness. With a better-structured timeline and more concise, well-designed presentations, these topics could be taught much earlier in the program, rather than being left to the fourth year.
assistant: Although the instructors involved in the course have different communication styles, I believe a common issue is inadequate communication competence. I observed a noticeably passive-aggressive attitude toward students, with a lack of appropriate respect; especially during juries/critiques, the tone often appears sarcastic, belittling, and condescending. When students react to such treatment, the response tends to become blaming rather than constructive. In my view, jury environments are far from a healthy and developmental space for academic critique; instead, they create a toxic atmosphere that is unprofessional, not aligned with academic standards, more accusatory than supportive, and ultimately demotivating for students. I am also concerned about fairness and impartiality in grading: while some students are treated respectfully and positively, others are addressed in ways that cross ethical boundaries, demeaning and, at times, arguably abusive. The perception of favoritism, and the impression that evaluations may be influenced by factors such as a student’s prior GPA or personal closeness to instructors, significantly undermines trust in academic fairness.
